metadata.title: A retrospective multicenter study of outcomes and complications in dogs undergoing total hip replacement with a BFX collared stem.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate outcomes and complications of the cementless BFX collared (BFX-C) stem in canine total hip replacement (THR) and identify risk factors for complications and subsidence. STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective multicenter study. ANIMALS: A total of 104 dogs undergoing 134 THR at four referral institutions (2019-2024). METHODS: Medical records and radiographs of dogs receiving a BFX-C stem were reviewed. Radiographic measurements included canal fill, canal flare index, stem alignment and subsidence. Clinical outcomes were assessed by orthopedic examination and owner questionnaire. Associations between putative risk factors and stem-specific complications and subsidence were assessed using univariable and multivariable analysis. RESULTS: Major stem-specific complications occurred in 15 (11.2%) procedures: intraoperative femoral fissures (7; 5.2%), intraoperative greater trochanter fractures (4; 3.0%), postoperative femoral fractures (3; 2.2%), subsidence requiring revision surgery (1; 0.8%). Median subsidence was 1.0 mm (range: -1.8-10.8). Subsidence of >3 mm in five (3.7%) cases, with one associated major complication. Increasing age was associated with greater subsidence (p = .04), but not with the likelihood of subsidence >3 mm (p = .08). At clinical follow-up (>3 months), 88/100 (88.0%) cases showed no lameness. Owners reported full limb function in 122 (91.0%) and acceptable function in 12 (9.0%) cases. CONCLUSION: The use of the BFX-C stem resulted in low rates of stem-specific complications and clinically relevant subsidence in this cohort. Subsidence ≤3 mm was common but not associated with stem-specific complications. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: The BFX-C stem is an acceptable option for cementless THR in dogs, providing high rates of full function and owner satisfaction.

metadata.title: Technical note: Combined approach for total mandibulectomy.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To describe a novel combined approach for total mandibulectomy (CATM) by combining a lateral approach for condylectomy and a ventral approach for total mandibulectomy. STUDY DESIGN: Descriptive technical note utilizing a cadaveric study and clinical case. ANIMALS: One dog cadaver (27 kg, mixed breed) and one clinical case (2.5-year-old castrated male Australian Shepherd). METHODS: The CATM technique was evaluated in a dog cadaver prior to clinical application in a dog with a left mandibular soft tissue sarcoma. Condylectomy was performed by a lateral approach to the temporomandibular joint followed by a ventral paramedian approach for left total mandibulectomy. RESULTS: CATM was successfully performed in both the cadaveric model and clinical case without intraoperative complications. Extending the lateral condylectomy incision caudally allowed for regional lymphadenectomy in the clinical case. Medial drift of the right mandible resulted in palatal contact trauma that was successfully managed with crown height reduction and vital pulpotomy. At two months postoperatively, the dog maintained good clinical function without tumor recurrence or additional adverse effects. CONCLUSION: The CATM was a feasible technique that provided increased TMJ exposure for joint disarticulation and condylectomy. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: The CATM provides a safe and effective technique for total mandibulectomy that optimizes TMJ access, facilitating joint disarticulation and condylectomy, while enhancing visualization of neurovascular structures.

metadata.title: Race Performance Following Arthroscopic Surgery for Femoropatellar and Tarsocrural Osteochondrosis in Juvenile Thoroughbreds.
metadata.journal: Veterinary and Comparative Orthopaedics and Traumatology
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The objective of this study is to evaluate racing performance of Thoroughbred yearlings following arthroscopic surgery for osteochondrosis (OC) of the femoropatellar (FP) and tarsocrural (TC) joints. STUDY DESIGN: This is a retrospective study of Thoroughbreds < 2 years old undergoing arthroscopic surgery for OC in the FP or TC joint (2010-2022). For each case, two age- and sex-matched controls from the same stud farm were selected. Lesions were graded on preoperative radiographs and described. Racing outcomes (number of starts, wins, places, podiums, prize money at 2nd, 3rd, and ≥4-year-old seasons, and career duration) were compared between groups using parametric or nonparametric tests according to data distribution (Student's t-test/analysis of variance or Mann-Whitney U/Kruskal-Wallis tests). RESULTS: A total of 49 horses included: 27 in the FP group and 22 in the TC group. In the FP group, the lateral trochlear ridge was most often affected; 14 were bilateral, two had OC lesions in another joint. In the TC group, the distal intermediate ridge of the tibia was mainly affected; five were bilateral and one had OC lesion in another joint. No significant differences were found between cases and controls in number of starts, wins, places, podiums, and prize money earned at 2nd, 3rd, and ≥4-year-old racing careers or career duration for either group (p > 0.05). In both groups, no significant performance differences were found between unilateral and bilateral cases (p > 0.05). CONCLUSION: Racing performance after FP or TC OC surgery was comparable to that of unaffected controls. Bilateral cases performed as successfully as unilateral.

metadata.title: Plasma Dimethylarginine Concentrations in Dogs With Large Cell Lymphoma or Hemangiosarcoma: A Prospective Observational Study.
metadata.abstract: Asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA) and symmetric dimethylarginine (SDMA) are endogenous methylated arginine derivatives associated with endothelial dysfunction and tumour progression in humans. Their relevance in canine oncology remains unclear. This prospective study aimed to assess plasma concentrations of ADMA and SDMA in dogs newly diagnosed with large cell lymphoma or non-cutaneous hemangiosarcoma (HSA); dogs with benign splenic lesions were also enrolled. Renal function was assessed at the time of inclusion to exclude overt kidney disease. Plasma ADMA and SDMA concentrations were measured at diagnosis, and clinical staging data were collected. A total of 31 dogs were enrolled: 11 with lymphoma, 15 with HSA and 5 with benign splenic lesions. SDMA concentrations exceeded the reference interval in 47%, 36% and 0% of dogs with HSA, lymphoma and benign lesions, respectively. Dogs with lymphoma (p = 0.003) and HSA (p = 0.013) had significantly higher SDMA concentrations than dogs with benign splenic lesions. Moreover, dogs with presumed disseminated HSA had significantly higher SDMA concentrations than those without metastatic disease (median: 21.5 vs. 12 μg/dL; p = 0.012). In contrast, plasma ADMA concentrations did not differ significantly among groups (p = 0.39). These findings suggest that lymphoma and HSA may represent extra-renal causes of SDMA elevation in dogs, and that SDMA could have value as a biomarker of tumour burden or progression. The potential clinical utility of ADMA in canine cancer warrants further investigation.

metadata.title: Prognostic characteristics of preoperative serum total bilirubin concentration in myxomatous mitral valve disease in dogs undergoing mitral valve repair.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: While serum total bilirubin concentration (Tbil) has emerged as a potential prognostic marker in dogs with myxomatous mitral valve disease (MMVD) after mitral valve repair (MVR), its dose-response relationship and underlying pathophysiological mechanisms remain unclear. HYPOTHESIS/OBJECTIVES: To characterize the dose-response relationships between preoperative Tbil and 2-year all-cause mortality after MVR and explore the role of right-sided cardiac compromise. ANIMALS: Two thousand sixty-three (cohort A) and 301 (cohort B) dogs with MMVD undergoing MVR at a single center. METHODS: This retrospective cohort study used multivariable Cox regression to assess the association between Tbil and 2-year mortality in cohort A. Cohort B evaluated relationships among Tbil, hepatic congestion, and right-sided overload. RESULTS: In cohort A, preoperative Tbil showed a linear positive association with 2-year all-cause mortality even within reference interval (ie, adjusted hazard ratio [0.3 vs. 0.1 mg/dL]: 1.33; 95% CI, 1.04-1.70). This association disappeared in dogs surviving beyond 30 days. Furthermore, higher preoperative Tbil levels were associated with an increased incidence of cardiac-related 30-day deaths in cohort A, and with right-sided cardiac overload at discharge in cohort B, which resolved by one month postoperatively. Hepatic congestion was associated with right-sided overload but not Tbil levels. CONCLUSIONS AND CLINICAL IMPORTANCE: Subtle preoperative Tbil elevations were associated with short-term all-cause mortality and transient right-sided overload, warranting careful interpretation even within reference intervals. However, the pathophysiological mechanism linking Tbil to postoperative prognosis remains to be elucidated. metadata.title: Seizures and blindness onset zone in 7 horses undergoing radiographic myelography in lateral recumbency under inhalation anesthesia.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Seizures and blindness are potential complications associated with myelography. HYPOTHESIS/OBJECTIVES: Describe, classify, and determine onset zone of seizures and blindness in horses undergoing radiographic myelography in lateral recumbency. ANIMALS: Seven young adult horses. METHODS: Retrospective study. Horses with seizures or blindness associated with myelography were included. RESULTS: Three horses with general proprioceptive ataxia and 4 neurologically normal horses (Warmblood = 4, Thoroughbred = 3), ages 9 (range, 3-16) years old. Iohexol (300 mg I/mL) from 50 to 60 mL (0.09-0.1 mL/kg) were administered intrathecally. Six horses had focal facial motor seizures contralateral to the side of recumbency with expansion to generalized seizures in one horse. The seizure onset zone was determined to be the right parietal cortex based on electroencephalography. Absent menace response of the left eye with bilateral normal dazzle and pupillary light reflexes were supportive of cortical blindness (right occipital cortex) in 5 horses. Seizures were managed using short- (diazepam, 3 horses; midazolam, 2; both, 1) and long-term (phenobarbital = 2/6) antiseizure medications with clinical resolution within 2-8 h post-myelogram. Blindness resolved within 8-48 h post-myelogram. CONCLUSIONS AND CLINICAL IMPORTANCE: Contralateral focal facial motor seizures and blindness with an onset zone in the parietal and occipital cerebral cortex, respectively, ipsilateral to the side of recumbency are possible adverse effects with characteristic features in horses undergoing radiographic myelography in lateral recumbency. These signs are transient with full resolution of seizures within hours and up to 2 days for the blindness.

metadata.title: Open versus minimally invasive surgical techniques for displaced abomasum in dairy cattle: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare open and minimally invasive surgical approaches for the treatment of abomasal displacement (AD) in dairy cows regarding effectiveness (mortality, recurrence, milk yield, and complications) and efficiency (operative time). Abomasal volvulus was not evaluated; thus, findings should not be extrapolated to that condition. STUDY DESIGN: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized and nonrandomized comparative studies conducted in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. SAMPLE POPULATION: Ten studies including 2900 dairy cows with AD, comprising three randomized controlled trials and seven nonrandomized comparative studies. METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for studies published through May 2025 comparing open and minimally invasive surgical techniques for AD. Outcomes assessed included mortality, operative time, recurrence, postoperative complications, and milk yield. Risk ratios (RR) and mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) were calculated using a random-effects model. Analyses were performed using Review Manager software (RevMan, version 5.4.1). RESULTS: In the pooled analysis of all 10 studies, minimally invasive surgery was associated with lower mortality (RR = 0.65; 95% CI 0.50-0.84; p = .001) and higher postoperative milk yield (MD = 1.76 kg/day; 95% CI 1.31-2.22; p < .00001) compared with open surgery. However, a sensitivity analysis restricted to the three randomized controlled trials showed no difference in mortality (RR = 1.27; 95% CI 0.39-4.07; p = .69), indicating that the overall mortality advantage was driven largely by nonrandomized studies. The milk yield result was similarly dependent on a single large observational study at serious risk of bias; excluding this study reduced the precision of the estimate (MD = 1.85 kg/day; 95% CI 0.09-3.60; p = .04), while the direction of the effect remained unchanged. No differences were found for operative time, recurrence, or complications, although the recurrence estimate was unstable in sensitivity analyses. CONCLUSION: Minimally invasive surgical techniques were associated with decreased mortality and improved milk production; however, these findings were driven predominantly by nonrandomized studies, and the mortality benefit was not confirmed in the randomized controlled trial (RCT)-only sensitivity analysis. Operative time, recurrence, and complication rates were similar between approaches. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: Minimally invasive procedures remain a reasonable option for the surgical management of AD in dairy cattle. However, because the supporting evidence is largely observational, a true survival or milk-yield advantage over open techniques cannot yet be considered established.

metadata.title: Comparison of coproparasitological diagnoses in cats: evaluation of techniques and their combinations.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare the Willis, Sheather, Faust, Ritchie and spontaneous sedimentation techniques, as well as their combinations, for the diagnosis of gastrointestinal parasites in domestic and semi-domesticated felines. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Coproparasitological analyses were conducted on domestic cats of both sexes and all age groups, including kittens, adults and senior cats, between August 2024 and August 2025. Upon receipt, they were refrigerated at 4°C and processed within a maximum of 24 hours using five different coproparasitological techniques. RESULTS: One hundred and fifteen samples were positive for at least one parasite form, with diagnoses of Toxocara spp., Ancylostomatidae, Dipylidium caninum, Spirometra spp., Platynosomum fastosum, Giardia spp., Cystoisospora spp. and Entamoeba spp. The Faust technique presented a superior range of diagnosis for low-density structures, whereas the Ritchie technique was effective for high-density structures. However, neither technique achieved a rate of at least 70%. Sensitivity analysis of the combination of these techniques revealed that: the Ritchie with spontaneous sedimentation technique was suitable for diagnosing toxocariasis and platynosomiasis; the Willis with Ritchie technique was appropriate for diagnosing hookworms; the Willis with Faust technique was suitable for diagnosing giardiasis; and the Sheather with Faust technique was appropriate for diagnosing cystoisosporiasis. It was not possible to analyse the association with other parasites owing to their low prevalence. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: Coproparasitological techniques remain the primary tools for diagnosing gastrointestinal parasites in routine feline practice, and the veterinarian's clinical suspicion is fundamental for performing the most appropriate technique. Considering the zoonotic potential of several parasites and frequent neglect of feline parasitosis, accurate diagnostic strategies and preventive veterinary practices are fundamental for reducing transmission in animals and humans.

metadata.title: Epidemiological, clinical and diagnostic aspects of feline otitis: a retrospective study of 103 cases from the dermatology service of a veterinary teaching hospital (2020-2022).
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To describe the epidemiological characteristics, clinical features, diagnostic findings and underlying causes of feline otitis in cases presented to a French veterinary teaching hospital. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Medical records of cats diagnosed with otitis by the dermatology department of a veterinary teaching hospital between September 2020 and March 2022 were retrospectively reviewed. Signalment, clinical history, video-otoscopic findings, cytology, imaging and histopathology results were collected. RESULTS: A total of 103 cats were diagnosed with otitis. Maine Coon, Sphynx, Turkish Angora and Selkirk Rex cats were significantly overrepresented. Age distribution showed increased case numbers in cats younger than 6 years, with another peak at 12 to 14 years of age. Chronic otitis represented 71.8% of cases. A primary cause was identified in 66.0% of cases, most frequently feline atopic syndrome, inflammatory polyps, neoplasia, isolated otitis media and otoacariasis. Staphylococcus spp. predominated in cultures (84.6%). Suppurative otitis was identified in 42 cats (40.8%). Video-otoscopy demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity for inflammatory polyps and otoacariasis. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: Feline otitis was predominantly chronic, with inflammatory polyps most commonly identified in younger cats and neoplasia in older cats; suppurative otitis was frequent and mainly associated with inflammatory polyps, otitis media and neoplasia. These findings emphasise the need for a comprehensive diagnostic approach to feline otitis, incorporating video-otoscopy and advanced imaging to identify age-related primary causes and guide clinical decision-making.

metadata.title: A single survey instrument reliably measures safety culture across 117 US primary and specialty care veterinary clinics.
metadata.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To validate an adapted version of the Nottingham Veterinary Safety Culture Survey in US private practice veterinary hospitals, encompassing primary and specialty care settings, and to characterize differences in safety culture perceptions among veterinary care worker populations. METHODS: A prospective cross-sectional safety culture survey was conducted between October 4 and November 24, 2023. Veterinary care workers of 123 VCA hospitals were invited to participate. The survey included 27 adapted statements from the original instrument. Confirmatory and exploratory factor analyses evaluated model performance. RESULTS: Responses were received from veterinary technicians or assistants (461 of 702 [65.7%]), other support staff (150 of 702 [21.4%]), and veterinarians (91 of 702 [13.0%]). Responses were received from primary care (502 [71.51%]), specialty care (137 [19.52%]), and hybrid hospitals (63 [8.97%]). Results of the confirmatory factor analysis showed adequately performing fit indices. Differences in responses were observed between leadership and nonleadership roles (75.86% of statements). Veterinarian responses differed from both veterinary technician and assistant (33.3%) and support staff (29.6%) roles. CONCLUSIONS: The psychometric properties of the Nottingham Veterinary Safety Culture Survey remain consistent when applied to a US private practice veterinary setting. Additionally, the adapted instrument, consisting of 27 statements, is appropriate for use across primary and specialty care hospital settings. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Safety culture is intrinsically linked to the safety of veterinary care workers and the patients in their care. Using validated survey instruments allows for assessment of safety culture that supports monitoring of potential intervention effectiveness and changes in patient and worker safety or health.

metadata.title: Diagnostic performance of 1,2-O-dilauryl-rac-glycero glutaric acid-(6'-methylresorufin) ester lipase activity in cats presenting to a veterinary referral hospital.
metadata.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To determine the prevalence of increased 1,2-O-dilauryl-rac-glycero glutaric acid-(6'-methylresorufin) ester (DGGR) lipase activity in cats with and without pancreatitis, and to evaluate its diagnostic performance relative to a clinical diagnosis of pancreatitis and ultrasonographic assessments. METHODS: Serum DGGR lipase activity was measured with the Randox lipase assay and considered increased if > 25 U/L. A board-certified internal medicine clinician, blinded to DGGR results, gave each cat a clinician-assigned score from 0 (no pancreatitis) to 4 (definite pancreatitis). Ultrasonographic scores (0 to 4) were assigned on the basis of the number of changes supportive of pancreatitis. DGGR lipase performance was compared with clinical and ultrasonographic scores. RESULTS: A total of 231 cats were included; 59 of 231 (25.5%) had increased DGGR lipase activity. Clinical scores were 0 in 47 of 231 cats (20.3%), 1 in 128 of 231 (55.4%), 2 in 36 of 231 (15.6%), and 3 in 20 of 231 (8.7%); no cats had a score of 4. With the use of a clinical score of 3 as the reference, DGGR lipase activity had a sensitivity of 70% and specificity of 79% (positive predictive value, 24%; negative predictive value, 97%). DGGR lipase activity was significantly lower in cats with an ultrasound score of 0 compared to scores of 1, 2, and 3. DGGR lipase activity was lower in cats with clinician-assigned scores of 0 and 1 compared to scores of 2 and 3. CONCLUSIONS: DGGR lipase activity was lower in cats with lower clinical and ultrasonographic scores and demonstrated a high negative predictive value. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: In this low-prevalence referral population, a normal DGGR lipase result reduced the likelihood of clinician-suspected pancreatitis.

metadata.title: Poorly concentrated urine is associated with an increased risk of developing chronic kidney disease in apparently healthy cats.
metadata.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate medical records from mature and senior cats stratified by urine specific gravity (USG; ≥ 1.035 or < 1.035) to examine the development of presumptive chronic kidney disease (CKD). METHODS: 15,027 apparently healthy cats were evaluated for inclusion in a 2-year longitudinal retrospective study. Outcome during the study period was a presumptive CKD diagnosis or development of creatinine > 1.6 mg/dL and USG < 1.035 with consistent clinical signs. Cats were grouped by age (mature, 11 to 15 years; senior, > 15 years) and USG values for contingency and survival analyses. A CKD assignment was precluded in cases where historical information, physical examination findings, diagnoses for each visit, and available diagnostic results over the study period contradicted a CKD diagnosis. RESULTS: 504 mature cats with a USG < 1.035, 1,872 mature cats with a USG ≥ 1.035, 89 senior cats with a USG < 1.035, and 149 senior cats with a USG ≥ 1.035 were included. In mature cats, contingency analysis using χ2 test found statistically significant differences in proportions of the population diagnosed presumptively with CKD during the study period, with an increased OR of 3.191 (CI, 1.611 to 6.231) as well as a shorter time to CKD diagnosis in the cats with USG < 1.035 at initial assessment. CONCLUSIONS: Identification of a USG < 1.035 appears to facilitate earlier renal disease detection and inform more individualized diagnostics in mature feline patients. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Identification of inadequate urine concentration in mature cats should raise concern for future renal disease detection and impact clinical assessment and monitoring.

metadata.title: Limb position, not exercise or sedation, affects power Doppler neovascularization detection in equine superficial digital flexor tendon core lesions.
metadata.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To determine the effect of limb position, exercise, and sedation on neovascularization detectability with the use of power Doppler ultrasonography (PDU) in superficial digital flexor tendon core lesions of the equine forelimb. METHODS: 9 Thoroughbred horses with superficial digital flexor tendon core tendinopathies were assessed with PDU before lesion induction (week 0) and 12 weeks after lesion induction, with 5 horses in the study period ranging from January to April 2024 and 4 horses from January to April 2025. During weeks 0 and 12, ultrasound examinations were performed 24 hours apart, with the limb weight-bearing and non-weight-bearing, before and after light exercise, and before and after IV detomidine sedation. The opposite forelimb served as a control. RESULTS: Limb position was the only variable with statistical significance. No blood flow was visualized in the prelesion surgical or control limb under all conditions. After lesion induction, neovascularization was significantly increased under all conditions when the limb was imaged during non-weight-bearing. CONCLUSIONS: Practitioners may utilize the information from this study to acknowledge the importance of non-weight-bearing limb position for neovascularization detection with PDU and may continue the standard exercise performed during a lameness examination and detomidine sedation administration to facilitate a complete diagnostic evaluation. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Light exercise, such as a typical lameness examination, and the administration of IV detomidine sedation to facilitate an ultrasound evaluation will not impact the detectability or degree of neovascularization with the use of PDU. Imaging the limb during non-weight-bearing will significantly increase the detectability and is a critical component of a complete evaluation.

metadata.title: Icterus in a 3-day-old Quarter Horse foal.
metadata.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association

metadata.title: High molecular weight adiponectin as an adjunct biomarker for insulin dysregulation in equids.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Total adiponectin concentration is associated with hyperinsulinemia and laminitis risk in ponies but the high molecular weight (HMW) multimer is a more sensitive indicator of metabolic disease in other species and could be a useful biomarker for insulin dysregulation (ID). HYPOTHESIS/OBJECTIVES: To determine a cut-off value for using HMW adiponectin as an adjunct diagnostic tool for ID. ANIMALS: Cohort of 127 privately and university-owned horses and ponies of various breeds with 55 classified as ID positive and 72 as ID negative. METHODS: Cohort study. Baseline and postprandial blood samples from an in-feed oral glucose test (0.75 g/kg dextrose) were used to determine ID status. Insulin and HMW adiponectin concentrations were measured using validated immunoassays. High molecular weight adiponectin cut-off values were derived with receiver-operator characteristic curve analysis using a bootstrap method to maximize the sum of sensitivity and specificity. RESULTS: Median [IQR] HMW adiponectin concentration was higher (P < .001) in ID negative animals (4.19 [2-6.5] μg/mL) compared to ID positive animals (1.79 [0.63-3.5] μg/mL), with a cut-off value (95% CI) of 2.1 (1.26, 3.15) μg/mL (area under the curve 0.71; sensitivity 0.62; and specificity 0.74). Horses had higher (P < .001) HMW adiponectin concentrations (4.38 [2.22-7.3] μg/mL) than ponies (1.84 [0.64-3.75] μg/mL). However, HMW adiponectin did not differ between horses with and without ID, and both horse subgroups had concentrations higher (P ≤ .002) than ponies with ID. CONCLUSIONS AND CLINICAL IMPORTANCE: Use of a single cut-off value for HMW adiponectin as an adjunct biomarker for ID for both horses and ponies is not accurate.

metadata.title: Association between cytology and endoscopy of guttural pouches: a prospective study on 173 horses.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Guttural pouch (GP) disorders are clinically important in horses, yet the relationship between endoscopic findings and GP cytology remains poorly defined. HYPOTHESIS/OBJECTIVES: To establish reference cytological values for GP lavage fluid in horses and to investigate associations between inflammatory cytology and endoscopic findings. ANIMAL: Asymptomatic racing horses sampled in the field and horses referred for investigation of respiratory disorders. METHODS: Prospective cross-sectional study. Horses underwent clinical examination, upper airway endoscopy, and bilateral transendoscopic GP lavage. A GP inflammation score (0-15) was developed based on endoscopic appearance in the GP. Cytology was performed on GP pooled samples. Control horses were defined by the absence of clinical, hematologic, microbiological, and endoscopic abnormalities. Associations were analyzed using nonparametric tests. RESULTS: A total of 173 horses were included, of which 19 were controls. Control GP fluid cytology exhibited no or rare cells (median 30 cells/mm3; range 10-90) which were either neutrophils, macrophages, or lymphocytes. The remaining 154 horses were classified as "abnormal" (ABN) and subdivided into 2 groups according to GP fluid neutrophil proportions: group ABN1 (<1% neutrophils, n = 101, median 30 cells/mm3; range 5-360) and group ABN2 (neutrophils ≥ 1%, n = 53, median 100 cells/mm3; range 30-600). Horses in the ABN2 group showed more frequent GP lymphoid hyperplasia, secretions, and purulent exudate than horses in ABN1. CONCLUSIONS AND CLINICAL IMPORTANCE: Cytological inflammation correlates with endoscopic evidence of GP inflammation.

metadata.title: Risk factors associated with lipaemic plasma in a cohort of canine blood donors.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To assess the prevalence of lipaemic plasma in healthy canine blood donors, identify predisposing factors, including dietary links and provide recommendations to reduce its occurrence. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A total of 296 healthy canine blood donors enrolled in a university blood bank were prospectively included. Health was confirmed through physical examination and complete bloodwork including total T4. After successful blood collection and processing, plasma intended for fresh frozen plasma production was assessed prior to freezing by two blinded operators using a turbidity/lipaemic index chart (0 = clear to 4 = opaque with severe lipaemia). Plasma units graded 3 to 4 (lipaemic) were compared with those graded 0 to 2 (non-lipaemic), and generalised linear models were used to identify risk factors for lipaemic plasma. RESULTS: The prevalence of lipaemic plasma in the donor cohort was 11.8%. Key associated factors included timing of the last meal (3.64 ± 0.95 vs. 5.94 ± 0.63 hours, P = .008), especially meals within 4 hours of collection (80.56 vs. 47.69%, P < .001 OR: 1.15), dietary fat content (46.8 ± 7.93 vs. 40.8 g/1000 kcal ± 1.09), feeding a raw diet (19.44% vs. 3.88%, P = .001 OR: 1.37) and triglyceridaemia (2.26 ± 0.36 vs. 0.91 ± 0.05 mmol/L, P < .001). CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: To minimise blood product loss due to lipaemic plasma, pre-collection guidelines may include a 4-hour fast and avoidance of fatty diets. This recommendation is particularly relevant for dogs fed a raw diet.

metadata.title: Occurrence of infections in dogs receiving ciclosporin in a single-centre UK referral population.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVES: The study aimed (a) to describe the occurrence and nature of new infections in dogs receiving oral ciclosporin and (b) to identify any risk factors associated with the development of a new infection whilst receiving ciclosporin. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this retrospective cohort study, medical records of dogs presented to a private UK referral hospital between March 2015 and September 2022 that received ciclosporin were evaluated. The development of a new infection was classified as confirmed or suspected, based on available data, and the infection was further characterised by causative agent (bacterial, fungal and parasitic) and location (integument, urogenital, hepatobiliary, cardiorespiratory, musculoskeletal and miscellaneous). Risk factors for the development of an infection were assessed using binary logistic regression analysis. RESULTS: Our cohort consisted of 265 dogs with 281 prescribed courses of ciclosporin. Of the included dogs, 33.2% (88/265) developed one or more new infections over the study period. When separated into aetiological groups, 26.0% of dogs (69/265) developed bacterial infections, 4.5% of dogs (12/265) developed fungal infections, 1.1% of dogs (3/265) developed parasitic infections, and 5.6% of dogs (15/265) developed unknown infections. Heavier dogs (increasing body weight OR 1.04, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.07), use of an additional third immunosuppressive agent (OR 1.96, 95% CI 1.09 to 3.51) and those receiving higher daily doses of ciclosporin (>8 mg/kg/day OR 3.01, 95% CI 1.41 to 6.46) were more likely to develop infections. The risk of infection was particularly increased with concurrent use of mycophenolate mofetil (OR 3.43; 95% CI 1.47 to 7.99). The most common locations for infection to occur in were the integument and urogenital systems. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: Increasing body weight, higher doses of ciclosporin and concurrent use of an additional third immunosuppressive agent, particularly mycophenolate, were risk factors for developing novel infections. The risks of ciclosporin treatment must be considered by the clinician and discussed with owners prior to use.

metadata.title: Serum peptidomic profiling identifies systemic JAK-STAT and PI3K-Akt pathway dysregulation in cats with chronic gingivostomatitis.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Chronic gingivostomatitis in cats is a debilitating inflammatory disease marked by severe oral pain and systemic immune dysregulation. Although localized oral pathology is well-documented, the systemic peptidomic profile remains largely unclear. HYPOTHESIS/OBJECTIVES: Characterize the serum peptidomic profiles of cats with feline chronic gingivostomatitis (FCGS) and identify systemic biomarkers and signaling hubs that drive disease pathogenesis and therapeutic interactions. ANIMALS: Client-owned cats with clinically and histopathologically confirmed FCGS (n = 34) and healthy controls (n = 18). METHODS: A case-control, cross-sectional study was conducted. All cats were screened for feline leukemia virus, feline immunodeficiency virus, and feline heartworm infections. Serum samples were analyzed using matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization-time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) to produce peptide mass fingerprints. Detailed peptide identification was conducted using nanoscale liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (nano LC-MS/MS). Functional enrichment and protein-protein/chemical interaction networks were developed using ShinyGO and the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes database. RESULTS: Both MALDI-TOF MS and nano LC-MS/MS identified distinct systemic protein signatures that distinguished FCGS from controls. Fifteen proteins showed significant changes, with 13 increased (including inflammatory markers such as interleukin (IL)-6 and interferon-γ) and 2 decreased (gastrin, IL-18). Network analysis identified 8 key proteins (eg, p21(CDKN1A), CASP1, IL-6) that interact with FCGS drug treatments. These systemic changes focus on the Janus kinase-signal transducers and activators of transcription (JAK-STAT) and phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT; PI3K-Akt) pathways, which are important therapeutic targets. CONCLUSIONS AND CLINICAL IMPORTANCE: Our study provides a molecular framework for FCGS. Whereas MALDI-TOF MS enables rapid systemic profiling, nano LC-MS/MS identifies key dysregulated pathways, specifically IL-6/JAK-STAT and PI3K-Akt. These findings offer potential therapeutic targets and a basis for monitoring molecular pathology in affected cats.

metadata.title: The effect of one-lung ventilation on sentinel lymph node mapping in dog lungs.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To determine the sentinel lymph node (SLN) for the caudal lung lobe using indocyanine green (ICG) and near infra-red fluorescence (NIRF) in normal dogs. The secondary objective was to determine the effect of one lung ventilation (OLV) on time to SLN detection. STUDY DESIGN: Prospective, randomized experimental study. ANIMALS: Purpose-bred Beagles (n = 21). METHODS: Dogs were randomized to undergo OLV or normal ventilation (NV) and to undergo right or left caudal lung injections with ICG through lateral intercostal thoracoscopy. The draining lymph nodes (DLNs) were visualized at 10 min intervals. RESULTS: A fluorescent lymph node (FLN) was detected in 19/21 dogs (90%) and was the right or left tracheobronchial lymph node (LN) in 79% of dogs. Six dogs had multiple FLNs detected simultaneously. In 4/19 dogs (21%) the first FLN(s) was the central tracheobronchial LN, sternal LN, cranial mediastinal LN or a combination of these LNs. The median time to fluorescence in the first FLN was 30 min (range: 10-50 min) for the OLV group and 10 min (range: 10-20 min) for the NV group (p = .0012). CONCLUSION: The SLN or DLN for the caudal lung in normal dogs was variable, but often included the tracheobronchial LN. One lung ventilation slowed the detection of ICG in the lymphatics. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: Biopsy of tracheobronchial LNs for caudal lung tumors without SLN mapping may provide inaccurate staging information in some dogs. During NIRF-guided SLN mapping, delaying OLV induction may improve SLN identification.

metadata.title: Prognosis and associated risk factors after conservative management of dogs with liver tumors.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Information is limited regarding prognosis for conservatively managed hepatic tumors in dogs. HYPOTHESIS/OBJECTIVES: Report prognosis and identify prognostic factors in dogs with conservatively managed hepatic tumors. ANIMALS: Client-owned dogs (n = 49) with hepatic tumors characterized by computed tomography (CT) without directed treatment that had died or were euthanized by the time of analysis. METHODS: Retrospective, single institutional study utilizing the Schwarzman Animal Medical Center medical record system to identify all dogs from 2013 to 2023 that met the inclusion criteria. Data collected included signalment, presenting complaints, blood test results, diagnosis, tumor imaging characteristics, and date of death. RESULTS: Median survival time from date of diagnosis was 313 days (range, 2-1308). Dogs with a presenting complaint of weight loss (P = .03) had a significantly shorter median survival time (128 days) than those without weight loss (341 days). Dogs presented with abdominal effusion (P = .03) had a significantly shorter median survival time (227 days) than dogs without effusion (331.5 days). Dogs with multiple hepatic masses (P = .004) had a significantly shorter median survival time (209.5 days) than dogs with a solitary mass (346 days). Higher aspartate aminotransferase (AST) activity and lower hematocrit (Hct) within 30 days of CT were associated with shorter median survival times (P = .02 and P = .01, respectively). Tumor volume/body weight ratio was not significantly related to survival time (P = .8). CONCLUSIONS AND CLINICAL IMPORTANCE: Poor prognostic factors for dogs with hepatic tumors include weight loss, abdominal effusion, multiple hepatic masses, increased AST activity, and low Hct.

metadata.title: Fluoroscopic characterization of pectus excavatum in dogs: a cross-sectional study.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: The dynamic respiratory abnormalities in dogs with pectus excavatum are incompletely characterized. HYPOTHESIS/OBJECTIVES: To characterize fluoroscopic findings in dogs with pectus excavatum and evaluate their associations with clinical severity. ANIMALS: Fifty-three client-owned dogs with pectus excavatum. METHODS: Cross-sectional study. Dogs were classified into low-severity or high-severity groups based on respiratory signs and treatment. Fluoroscopic examinations were evaluated for pectus excavatum-intrinsic findings and concurrent respiratory abnormalities. Associations with clinical severity were assessed using univariable and multivariable analyses. RESULTS: Multiple fluoroscopic findings of pectus excavatum were characterized. Paradoxical sternal movement was independently associated with clinical severity (odds ratio [OR] 3.71, 95% CI, 1.03-13.4; P = .045). Thoracic height reduction ratio was significantly higher in the high-severity group (0.140 [IQR, 0.100-0.228]) compared with the low-severity group (0.097 [IQR, 0.064-0.133]; P = .04). Mainstem bronchial collapse was present in all dogs (53/53, 100%) and cervical lung lobe herniation in 50/53 (94%; 95% CI, 84%-99%). Most other fluoroscopic variables showed no significant associations with clinical severity. CONCLUSIONS AND CLINICAL IMPORTANCE: Paradoxical sternal movement, particularly with greater thoracic height reduction, may serve as a supportive indicator of clinical severity. The high prevalence of bronchial collapse and cervical lung lobe herniation suggests an association between pectus excavatum and these airway abnormalities in dogs.

metadata.title: Successful immunosuppressive treatment of hypersensitivity pneumonitis secondary to lycoperdonosis in a dog.
metadata.abstract: A 7-year-old neutered male Cocker Spaniel with unrestricted access to rural land presented for progressive lethargy, tachypnea, and cough. Thoracic radiographs showed an unstructured interstitial pattern. Fine-needle aspirate (FNA) lung cytology identified pyogranulomatous inflammation with intralesional mushroom spores. Acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP) was suspected, and treatment was initiated with oxygen supplementation and an immunosuppressive dosage of corticosteroid. Thoracic computed tomography (CT) and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) were performed on day 6, month 2, and year 1 to track therapeutic response and assess architectural changes. Clinical signs guided prednisone tapering and discontinuation. One year later, thoracic CT and BAL confirmed re-exposure to mushroom spores with mild persistent inflammation and CT changes suggestive of mixed parenchymal and small airway disease despite absent clinical signs. This case report emphasizes the importance of rapid identification of pulmonary mushroom spores for prompt immunosuppressive treatment. Unlike prior reports of lycoperdonosis with acute, fulminating, and generally fatal outcomes, this dog developed chronic HP.

metadata.title: Association of electrolyte concentrations with pH of blood and urine of cows with left-sided abomasal displacement.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Ruminants with left-sided abomasal displacement (LDA) often develop metabolic alkalosis and paradoxical aciduria. HYPOTHESIS/OBJECTIVES: To descriptively characterize electrolytes and acid-base variables in cows with LDA compared to healthy cows using the physicochemical (Stewart) approach, and to exploratively assess the influence of blood and urinary electrolytes on pH. ANIMALS: Twenty healthy dairy cows and 20 cows with LDA. METHODS: Retrospective cross-sectional study. Electrolytes, pH, total protein (TP), β-hydroxybutyrate (BHB), and glucose were measured in venous blood and urine. Base excess, anion gap, strong ion difference (SID), and strong ion gap (SIG) were calculated. Associations were evaluated using 2 stepwise forward multiple linear regression models. RESULTS: Cows with LDA had significantly lower venous concentrations of sodium, chloride, potassium, magnesium, and calcium (P = .0013, P = .0023, P < .001, P < .001, P < .001), higher BHB (P < .001), and higher blood pH (P = .003) compared to controls. Calculated SID3, SID4, SID5, and SIG did not differ significantly between groups (P = .2, P = .37, P = .40, P = .62). In urine, cows with LDA showed significantly lower concentrations of Na+, K+, Cl-, Mg2+, and HCO₃- (P = .0007, P < .001, P < .001, P = .004, P < .001). Urinary SID3 and SID5 were also significantly lower (both P < .001). CONCLUSIONS AND CLINICAL IMPORTANCE: Acid-base disturbances in cows with LDA can be interpreted using the physicochemical approach. Alterations in electrolyte concentrations contribute to changes in pH.

metadata.title: Bartonella vinsonii subsp. berkhoffii genotype III in a dog with recurrent fever and panniculitis coinfected with Babesia odocoilei-like sp.
metadata.abstract: A 2-year-old, spayed female, mixed breed dog presented for evaluation of recurrent febrile episodes over 5 months, intermittently accompanied by the development of SC nodules. Histopathologic examination of the SC lesions was indicative of panniculitis. Bartonella vinsonii subsp. berkhoffii genotype III DNA was amplified and sequenced from an excised SC nodule. Indirect immunofluorescence antibody titer was 1:64, whereas Bartonella blood PCR was negative. Babesia odocoilei-like species DNA was amplified and sequenced from 2 blood samples obtained 77 days apart at the time of febrile episodes. Treatment with doxycycline, enrofloxacin, and azithromycin for 6 months resulted in a favorable clinical outcome. Fifteen months later, the dog remained healthy. This case indicates that relapsing fever and panniculitis are possible manifestations of B vinsonii subsp. berkhoffii genotype III infection in dogs. To the best of the authors' knowledge, infection with a B odocoilei-like species has not been reported previously in dogs from Greece.

metadata.title: Depth and distribution of colonic sand accumulation in a desert population of horses and its association with diagnosis of sand colic.
metadata.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To describe patient and management characteristics associated with radiographic sand accumulation in a desert population of horses, as well as identify factors independently associated with a diagnosis of sand colic and need for surgical intervention. METHODS: Horses were prospectively allocated into 3 groups: control horses, horses with sand colic, and horses with non-sand-associated colic. Signalment, radiographs, and management outcomes were compared between groups. RESULTS: Median depth of sand was significantly greater in horses diagnosed with sand colic compared to other groups (112.16 vs 10.5 vs 12.0 mm). Increasing sand depth was associated with increased odds of having sand colic. Younger horses were more likely to be diagnosed with sand colic (2 vs 4.9 years); however, surgical intervention was more likely in older horses (2.6 vs 1.3 years). CONCLUSIONS: Horses diagnosed with sand colic exhibited greater sand depth compared to those with non-sand colic or controls. For every millimeter of sand present, horses had a 2% increase in the odds of being diagnosed with sand colic. Factors independently associated with a diagnosis of sand colic were a lower body weight, presence of cranial sand on radiographs, and increasing sand depth. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The OR of a diagnosis of sand colic increases by 2% with every millimeter of measured sand depth. Additionally, greater depths of sand were not associated with increased risk of surgical management. This data helps clinicians determine the relevance of sand identified radiographically in horses presenting for colic.

metadata.title: Pet-ownership inquiry and cross-species referral are clinically relevant priorities for human and veterinary medical care providers: a cross-sectional survey.
metadata.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To assess the importance human and veterinary providers and nonproviders place on One Health interprofessional collaboration and identify factors associated with provider comfort in making cross-species referrals. METHODS: An online, cross-sectional survey was given to human and veterinary providers via professional associations and snowball sampling (January to February 2025) and to nonproviders via a nationally representative panel. Analyses included frequencies, ordinal logistic regression, and χ2 tests. RESULTS: A total of 1,660 respondents were enrolled (144 human providers, 50 veterinary providers, 1,466 nonproviders). Among human providers, pet ownership was associated with higher importance for pet-ownership inquiry (OR, 3.44; range, 1.53 to 7.70), cross-species care inquiry (OR, 2.29; range, 1.09 to 4.78), and greater comfort making cross-species referrals (OR, 2.18; range, 1.04 to 4.57). Specialty human providers assigned lower importance to both inquiries versus primary human providers, with ORs of 0.46 (range, 0.21 to 1.00) and 0.45 (range, 0.21 to 0.98), respectively. Among veterinary providers, viewing client health as a proxy for patient health was statistically significantly associated with greater referral comfort (OR, 4.39; range, 1.11 to 17.36). CONCLUSIONS: Pet ownership among human providers is the strongest predictor of engagement with One Health inquiry and referral. Specialty human providers are a key gap One Health training opportunity. Veterinary providers who frame client wellness as relevant to patient health show markedly higher comfort with client referral to a human provider. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Questions about pet ownership and cross-species health may yield relevant insights for providers. Incorporating One Health inquiries into standard intakes could improve patient/client outcomes and advance interprofessional collaboration.

metadata.title: Feasibility of bone-targeted electrochemotherapy for palliation of bone tumors in dogs and cats.
metadata.journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association
metadata.abstract: Electrochemotherapy (ECT) is a minimally invasive locoregional treatment that combines reversible electroporation with cytotoxic agents to enhance intracellular drug delivery. Although its efficacy is well established in cutaneous malignancies, its role in bone tumors has only recently been explored in veterinary medicine. This narrative review integrates preclinical evidence, human clinical data, and early veterinary experience with an original 4-case series to evaluate the translational potential of ECT in bone oncology. Preclinical studies demonstrate effective tumor ablation within bone while preserving extracellular matrix integrity and enabling bone tissue regeneration. Clinical studies in humans report consistent pain relief, meaningful local tumor control, and acceptable safety profiles, including in complex scenarios, such as radiotherapy-resistant metastatic epidural spinal cord compression. In contrast, veterinary evidence remains limited to isolated case reports, in part due to limited dedicated technologies. Taken together, available data suggest that ECT may represent a function-preserving alternative for selected bone tumors. Prospective studies are warranted to define its clinical role in veterinary medicine.
